hird.name: Hirdman
hird.prompt:
Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Norse look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but colder and harder than the Greek cards. Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Norse look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but colder and harder than the Greek cards. Heavier, rougher black ink lines with a carved, woodcut-like quality, as if cut into wood or stone; flat areas of colour broken by scratchy hatching. A northern base of slate, iron grey, bone white and pine, but every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that dominates the picture: bold and saturated, such as deep blood red, aurora green and violet, velvet purple, ember orange, glacier blue or midnight-sun gold, so the cards never all read as grey-blue. No warm Mediterranean light, no sunsets over a warm sea, no bronze glow. Weather matters: snow, sleet, sea-spray, mist and long winter dusk. Where the picture shows objects, give them Viking Age ornament: interlaced beasts and knotwork carved on wood, iron and runestones in the Urnes and Mammen styles, and the look of the Gotland picture-stones. People are weathered and heavy, in wool, fur, leather and iron; no horned helmets, no winged helmets, no fantasy plate armour. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Viking Age Norse myth: iron mail, round wooden shields, furs, runestones, longhalls, ravens, wolves, fjords, snow and northern sky.

Subject: The rimewall: a towering wall of blue glacier ice blocking a mountain pass, with huge frost giants dimly visible inside the ice like shadows.

Composition: the main subject partly in silhouette against light, at a dramatic tilted angle. Light and colour: pale ice blue and bone. Presence: an overwhelming, mythic sight. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.

composition.shot: the main subject partly in silhouette against light

Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Norse look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but colder and harder than the Greek cards. Heavier, rougher black ink lines with a carved, woodcut-like quality, as if cut into wood or stone; flat areas of colour broken by scratchy hatching. A northern base of slate, iron grey, bone white and pine, but every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that dominates the picture: bold and saturated, such as deep blood red, aurora green and violet, velvet purple, ember orange, glacier blue or midnight-sun gold, so the cards never all read as grey-blue. No warm Mediterranean light, no sunsets over a warm sea, no bronze glow. Weather matters: snow, sleet, sea-spray, mist and long winter dusk. Where the picture shows objects, give them Viking Age ornament: interlaced beasts and knotwork carved on wood, iron and runestones in the Urnes and Mammen styles, and the look of the Gotland picture-stones. People are weathered and heavy, in wool, fur, leather and iron; no horned helmets, no winged helmets, no fantasy plate armour. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Viking Age Norse myth: iron mail, round wooden shields, furs, runestones, longhalls, ravens, wolves, fjords, snow and northern sky.

Subject: An ember sprite: a small, flickering fire spirit shaped like a laughing imp made of embers and sparks, darting over glowing coals.

Composition: the creature filling the whole frame, head close to the viewer, from slightly above. Light and colour: molten forge gold and red. Presence: a dangerous but ordinary foe. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.

composition.shot: the creature filling the whole frame, head close to the viewer

Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Norse look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but colder and harder than the Greek cards. Heavier, rougher black ink lines with a carved, woodcut-like quality, as if cut into wood or stone; flat areas of colour broken by scratchy hatching. A northern base of slate, iron grey, bone white and pine, but every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that dominates the picture: bold and saturated, such as deep blood red, aurora green and violet, velvet purple, ember orange, glacier blue or midnight-sun gold, so the cards never all read as grey-blue. No warm Mediterranean light, no sunsets over a warm sea, no bronze glow. Weather matters: snow, sleet, sea-spray, mist and long winter dusk. Where the picture shows objects, give them Viking Age ornament: interlaced beasts and knotwork carved on wood, iron and runestones in the Urnes and Mammen styles, and the look of the Gotland picture-stones. People are weathered and heavy, in wool, fur, leather and iron; no horned helmets, no winged helmets, no fantasy plate armour. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Norse look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but colder and harder than the Greek cards. Heavier, rougher black ink lines with a carved, woodcut-like quality, as if cut into wood or stone; flat areas of colour broken by scratchy hatching. A northern base of slate, iron grey, bone white and pine, but every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that dominates the picture: bold and saturated, such as deep blood red, aurora green and violet, velvet purple, ember orange, glacier blue or midnight-sun gold, so the cards never all read as grey-blue. No warm Mediterranean light, no sunsets over a warm sea, no bronze glow. Weather matters: snow, sleet, sea-spray, mist and long winter dusk. Where the picture shows objects, give them Viking Age ornament: interlaced beasts and knotwork carved on wood, iron and runestones in the Urnes and Mammen styles, and the look of the Gotland picture-stones. People are weathered and heavy, in wool, fur, leather and iron; no horned helmets, no winged helmets, no fantasy plate armour. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Viking Age Norse myth: iron mail, round wooden shields, furs, runestones, longhalls, ravens, wolves, fjords, snow and northern sky.

Subject: Loki's toll: a grinning Loki holding out his open palm for payment at a narrow bridge, a pile of gold rings at his feet.

Composition: a dramatic close-up of one telling detail, from directly above. Light and colour: aurora violet and teal. Presence: an overwhelming, mythic sight. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.

composition.shot: a dramatic close-up of one telling detail

Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Norse look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but colder and harder than the Greek cards. Heavier, rougher black ink lines with a carved, woodcut-like quality, as if cut into wood or stone; flat areas of colour broken by scratchy hatching. A northern base of slate, iron grey, bone white and pine, but every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that dominates the picture: bold and saturated, such as deep blood red, aurora green and violet, velvet purple, ember orange, glacier blue or midnight-sun gold, so the cards never all read as grey-blue. No warm Mediterranean light, no sunsets over a warm sea, no bronze glow. Weather matters: snow, sleet, sea-spray, mist and long winter dusk. Where the picture shows objects, give them Viking Age ornament: interlaced beasts and knotwork carved on wood, iron and runestones in the Urnes and Mammen styles, and the look of the Gotland picture-stones. People are weathered and heavy, in wool, fur, leather and iron; no horned helmets, no winged helmets, no fantasy plate armour. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Viking Age Norse myth: iron mail, round wooden shields, furs, runestones, longhalls, ravens, wolves, fjords, snow and northern sky.

Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Chinese look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but painted in the manner of classical Chinese painting and the illustrated Ming editions of Journey to the West. Fluid, calligraphic brush lines that swell and taper, never hard woodcut or pen hatching. Figures in the fine-line gongbi manner with flat, bold mineral colours (cinnabar red, azurite blue, malachite green, gold) on a warm rice-paper ground; backgrounds in loose xieyi ink wash: misty peaks, pines, waterfalls, splashed ink. Clouds are drawn as curling auspicious-cloud scrolls. Faces and poses are bold and theatrical, like Peking opera. Every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that dominates the picture. Not Japanese, not samurai, not anime, not modern Chinese fantasy game art, no restaurant-style dragons. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Journey to the West, classical Chinese myth: silk robes, lacquered armour, temples, clouds, mountains, celestial palaces.

Subject: The dramatic moment of the spell "Staff Smash" taking effect (strike · spell). What it does in the game, for mood only: Deal 2 damage to target opposing army member and 1 damage to each other opposing army member.

Composition: the effect swirling around a single figure, close up, from a low angle. Light and colour: smoky violet dusk. Presence: an imposing, dramatic presence with strong rim light. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.

composition.shot: the effect swirling around a single figure, close up
composition.power: an imposing, dramatic presence with strong rim light

Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Chinese look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but painted in the manner of classical Chinese painting and the illustrated Ming editions of Journey to the West. Fluid, calligraphic brush lines that swell and taper, never hard woodcut or pen hatching. Figures in the fine-line gongbi manner with flat, bold mineral colours (cinnabar red, azurite blue, malachite green, gold) on a warm rice-paper ground; backgrounds in loose xieyi ink wash: misty peaks, pines, waterfalls, splashed ink. Clouds are drawn as curling auspicious-cloud scrolls. Faces and poses are bold and theatrical, like Peking opera. Every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that dominates the picture. Not Japanese, not samurai, not anime, not modern Chinese fantasy game art, no restaurant-style dragons. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Journey to the West, classical Chinese myth: silk robes, lacquered armour, temples, clouds, mountains, celestial palaces.

Subject: A still-life or place: "Cobweb", a sacred object or site lit like a relic (opening trump). What it does in the game, for mood only: Ward. The first army member that attacks each turn does not untap next turn.

Composition: a dramatic close-up of one telling detail, from directly above. Light and colour: celestial gold on deep blue. Presence: an overwhelming, mythic sight. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.

composition.shot: a dramatic close-up of one telling detail
